title: War, Race, and America’s Values
gist: A review of Wil Haygood's 'The War Within a War' that uses Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's anti-DEI West Point commencement speech — delivered moments before a Black class president handed him the cadet saber — as the frame for arguing that military personnel policy has always functioned as America's litmus test for its own values. The essay traces Vietnam-era disproportionate Black combat assignment, racialized draft boards, Project 100,000, and the Johnson-Russell bargain that traded War on Poverty funding for defense spending.

themes.theme: Hegseth's West Point address and its immediate contradiction

insights.claim: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the West Point graduating class that 'Our diversity is our strength' was the single dumbest phrase in military history, instructed cadets not to see color or celebrate identity months, and equated diversity and inclusion studies with anti-American ideologies.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Establishes that the Pentagon's top civilian is using service-academy commencements as an explicit ideological platform — a signal of how far personnel policy has become a partisan front.
insights.quote: the single dumbest phrase in military history
insights.locator: To the assembled West Point Corps of Cadets

insights.claim: Hegseth linked an obsession with race and gender directly to a watering down of discipline, a causal claim the review characterizes as mendacious.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The discipline-erosion argument is the load-bearing justification for dismantling military diversity programs, so contesting it is where the policy fight actually turns.
insights.locator: Hegseth railed against an "obsession with race and gender"

insights.claim: Minutes after that speech, Hegseth received the traditional framed cadet saber from class president Miles Manney, a Black cadet who served as brigade information systems officer, earned a minor in terrorism studies, and taught Protestant Sunday school.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The juxtaposition is the essay's central rhetorical device: the individual record refutes the quota framing in the same frame as the speech.

insights.claim: The Hegseth speech drew muted Republican Party pushback, indicating the position now sits inside rather than outside the party mainstream.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Absence of intra-party friction implies these personnel policies will persist rather than be walked back.
insights.locator: If the secretary's oration was unsurprising

insights.claim: The Trump administration purged websites of notable Black and female achievements in the military, fired Charles Q. Brown from the chairmanship of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and renamed Fort Gregg-Adams back to Fort Lee, reversing recognition of the Army's first Black lieutenant general.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Concrete, reversible-in-principle administrative actions that mark how quickly institutional memory can be redirected by executive preference.
insights.quote: cadre of gifted Black military leaders
insights.locator: Haygood ends his story with both Secretary Hegseth and President Trump

insights.claim: Two conflicts unfolded simultaneously during the 1960s — the war in Vietnam and an existential struggle over American identity at home — with race at the center of both and each inseparable from the other.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: A reusable frame for reading any war-era society: overseas conflict and domestic legitimacy struggles are one system, not two.
insights.locator: In essence, two conflicts unfolded simultaneously

insights.claim: Black recruits were sent into combat units in Vietnam at a disproportionately higher rate than White soldiers, while local draft boards, especially in the American South, granted service deferments based more on color than on need.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Documents how an ostensibly neutral conscription system distributed lethal risk along racial lines through local administrative discretion.
insights.locator: We see Black recruits being sent into combat units

insights.claim: Young Black men enlisted primarily because of economic necessity and limited employment opportunities in America's inner cities of the 1960s, making military service a labor-market decision as much as a patriotic one.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The economic-conscription mechanism still governs who fills the ranks — recruitment tracks local opportunity, not ideology.
insights.locator: We empathize with young Black men and their families

insights.claim: Activists including James Baldwin, Muhammad Ali and Martin Luther King Jr. explicitly likened the bombing of Vietnamese villages to the violence meted out in Black neighborhoods across the United States.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Shows the anti-war and civil rights arguments were fused at the rhetorical level, not merely coincident movements.
insights.locator: And we listen to activists such as James Baldwin

insights.claim: President Johnson reluctantly but purposefully diminished funding for his War on Poverty to compensate for a ballooning defense budget supporting an increasingly stalemated Vietnam conflict, while segregationist Senate Armed Services chairman Richard Russell — who voted against the 1964 Civil Rights Act — gave Johnson everything he needed to prosecute the war.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The classic guns-versus-butter trade in its sharpest historical form: war spending crowded out the domestic program that was supposed to deliver on civil rights.
insights.locator: In another chapter, Haygood demonstrates breadth of scope

themes.theme: Service as a litmus test for American values

insights.claim: Historian William A. Taylor argued that uniformed service functions as a litmus test for American values and that military personnel policies have served as the nation's conscience, bringing uncomfortable questions about American values into sharp relief.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Explains why fights over military DEI carry outsized political weight: personnel policy is where national values get adjudicated concretely.
insights.quote: served as the nation’s conscience, bringing difficult and uncomfortable questions about American values into sharp relief

insights.claim: The assumption that military service would earn expanded civil rights predates Vietnam: W.E.B. Du Bois applauded Black participation in World War I as a route to full citizenship, then judged the result a betrayal as the government reinforced Jim Crow at war's end.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The service-for-rights bargain has failed repeatedly, which is the historical basis for skepticism about institutional promises of meritocracy.
insights.locator: During World War I, scholar and civil rights activist W.E.B. Du Bois

insights.claim: The record supports both readings of the litmus test simultaneously — genuine meritocracy in the careers of Joe Anderson, Fred Cherry and Art Gregg, alongside Project 100,000 conscription of the poor and less-educated, unfair courts-martial, Agent Orange, and Medal of Honor recipient Dwight Johnson's death while attempting a robbery in Detroit.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Refuses the single-narrative framing that both political camps rely on — the institution has been simultaneously the most integrated and the most extractive.
insights.locator: Yet alongside these inspiring stories sit tales

insights.claim: Only 23 Black servicemembers received the Medal of Honor in Vietnam, and one of them, Dwight Johnson, suffered post-traumatic stress and was fatally shot in Detroit while trying to rob a grocery store.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The clearest single data point on the gap between wartime recognition and postwar support for veterans.
insights.locator: Dwight Johnson, one of only 23 Black recipients

insights.claim: The era posed questions the military never cleanly answered: whether the 'dap' handshake among African American soldiers was cultural esprit de corps or an affront to order and discipline, and whether fighting communism abroad mattered more than resolving racial inequities at home.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The same discipline-versus-identity argument Hegseth deploys today was already being litigated in Vietnam over a handshake.
insights.locator: Contradictions abound in these personal stories

insights.claim: One of the era's most alarming institutional anxieties was that young Black men conscripted and trained to kill would become a potential threat to American society once they returned from Vietnam.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Reveals that the state's fear of its own veterans shaped race policy — an underexamined driver of postwar domestic security posture.

insights.claim: Time correspondent Wallace Terry documented growing political consciousness among Black troops in Vietnam from 1967 and produced 'Bloods', an oral history that remains an indispensable resource for historians of the conflict.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Identifies the primary-source lineage on which the contemporary account rests — useful for anyone assessing the evidentiary base of these claims.
insights.locator: In one illustrative chapter, Haygood turns his attention to Wallace Terry

themes.theme: Method and verdict on the book

insights.claim: Haygood departs from institutional histories such as Beth Bailey's work on the military's approach to the 'problem of race' by concentrating on individuals, producing a social and cultural rather than policy rendering of the era.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: Method matters for what the book can prove: individual narrative persuades but does not settle contested institutional questions.
insights.locator: Complementing the work of historians before him

insights.claim: American martial history cannot be told without its history of race, and war and race are inseparable from the American story.
insights.speaker: Lawfare Blog
insights.so_what: The reviewer's core claim, positioned directly against the current Pentagon leadership's stated position.
insights.quote: he shows us how war and race are inseparable from the American story
insights.locator: In the end, being swept up in a narrative
